title: Rippling MCP Server Setup and Access Permissions
summary: Rippling MCP connects AI clients to Rippling via the Model Context Protocol. Permissions control access; know setup requirements and common errors.
body_markdown:
## Where Activepieces Fits Next to Rippling MCP


### When the work runs unattended


When the work is the kind nobody's watching,[Activepieces](https://www.activepieces.com/) fits, and it carries unlimited flows on every plan, including free, so one flow per Rippling event never runs into a flow quota.


That means a workflow that runs when a Rippling event fires, while Rippling MCP stays the tool for a person asking questions and checking the answer. That split follows from the rule above.


When someone compares a figure with Rippling's report, a human's in the loop. A new-hire alert has no such step, so it shouldn't depend on a chat session.


### The two lanes side by side


Side by side, the two lanes look like the illustration below. In the first, a person at a laptop asks a chat client connected to Rippling MCP, reads the reply, and decides what to do with it.


In the second lane, a Rippling new-hire event feeds an Activepieces workflow that posts an alert to Slack, the team chat tool, with no one asking anything.


A run costs 1 credit however many steps it has, and the free plan includes 1,000 credits a month.


Take from it that the lanes differ in who's accountable at the moment of action: in the first it's the person reading, in the second it's whoever owns the workflow.


That's the question to settle before building anything. When the alert fails at 2am on a Tuesday, someone gets paged, and it needs to be a named owner rather than whoever last edited the flow.


### Rippling permissions to check before building workflows


Because a workflow acts under a stored credential, the permissions behind that connection matter as much as the ones you verified for MCP. Check them in Rippling's documentation, and scope the workflow to the one event it needs.


The Rippling connection is where the risk sits, and an SDK gives an agent code to run without giving it a tenant, a role or an audit log.


Activepieces treats the agent as a user: SSO and standard roles come with the Team plan at $200 a month, SCIM, custom RBAC and audit logs with Ultimate, and run history and a step-by-step trace of what the agent decided and which tool it called, plus log streaming into the tools your security team already watches, so agent activity appears in the same logs as any other system event.


Before you design around Activepieces, know that MoneyGram, Moneypenny, Alan and FundingSocieties run it, and that its open source repository holds 750 integrations.


Confirm the specific triggers and actions in its connector listing, because a connector name doesn't tell you which Rippling data it can read or change.


Activepieces doesn't replace Rippling MCP. It gives scheduled or event-driven work a place to run, with a run history you can review, which a chat conversation doesn't. The free self-hosted Community Edition is MIT-licensed, so you can try that split without a contract.
